paper_title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

Introduction Diffusion and flow matching models have achieved remarkable success in high-quality image [6, 10], video [50], and audio [22] generation. However, their iterative sampling processes typically require tens of network evaluations, resulting in substantial inference costs. Few-step distillation addresses this limitation by transferring the generative capabilities of pretrained teacher into student that requires only one or few denoising steps [19, 40, 44, 49]. Among existing approaches, distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as one of the most effective and widely adopted paradigms [33, 62]. While DMD has demonstrated impressive one-step generation capabilities, single network evaluation often struggles to preserve fine-grained details and complex structures [61]. Recent methods therefore extend DMD to multi-step generation, allowing the student to progressively refine its predictions and achieve higher generation quality while maintaining efficient inference [21, 23, 34, 61]. The central idea of DMD is to train the student by minimizing the distributional discrepancy between its generated samples and those of the pretrained teacher. Specifically, DMD formulates this objective through the reverse KullbackLeibler (KL) divergence between their noiseperturbed distributions, whose gradient can be estimated from the difference between the teachers and students score functions [62]. Since the students score is not directly available, DMD introduces an auxiliary diffusion model, known as the fake score model, which is trained online on student-generated samples to approximate the students distribution. The discrepancy between the teachers prediction, often enhanced with classifier-free guidance (CFG) [9], and the fake models estimate then provides the correction signal for updating the student. Importantly, the distribution learned by the fake model determines the reference against which the student is optimized. When denoising is performed in single step, the students prediction is also its final generated output, making the distribution learned by the fake model naturally consistent with the desired matching objective. When denoising involves multiple steps, however, the student produces sequence of intermediate predictions before generating its final output. These predictions generally follow different distributions, so how the fake model is trained becomes central design choice. Existing multi-step DMD methods incorporate intermediate predictions or states into the training of the fake model  (Fig. 2)  , following two paradigms. The first, represented by DMD2 [61], trains shared fake model using predictions collected from different denoising steps, effectively learning mixture of intermediate and final prediction distributions. The second, represented by TDM [34], constructs stage-dependent references from intermediate denoising states and performs distribution matching within their corresponding noise intervals. Despite their different implementations, both paradigms couple the distribution matching objective to intermediate distributions, whereas the ultimate goal of distillation is to match the students final output distribution to the teachers. This distinction is particularly important for few-step students, which compress complex generative process into only few steps. Their intermediate predictions need not follow the teachers corresponding distributions, even when their final outputs accurately reproduce the teachers distribution. Therefore, imposing distributional constraints on intermediate predictions may introduce unnecessary restrictions and interfere with the optimization of final generation quality. teacher enhancement To understand the consequences of this mismatch, we theoretically analyze how the fake models reference distribution influences the student update. We denote the distribution of the students final outputs as the endpoint distribution. Under exact conditional denoisers, we decompose the DMD correction signal into three components term arising from (Eq. (3)): guidance, an endpoint matching term that measures the discrepancy between the teacher and the students final output distribution, and an additional reference residual caused by the discrepancy between the fake models reference distribution and the endpoint distribution. Our analysis reveals that existing intermediate-based references can introduce nonzero residual that fundamentally changes the intended distribution matching behavior. Even when the students final output distribution already matches the teachers, this residual may remain nonzero and continue to push the student away from the desired distribution. We further prove that the reference residual vanishes if and only if the fake model represents the endpoint distribution, regardless of intermediate distributions (Prop. 1). Our two-dimensional synthetic experiments confirm these effects, showing that intermediate-based references deflect the update from the desired direction, whereas an endpoint-aligned reference does not  (Fig. 3)  . the students These findings motivate simple principle: the fake 2 Figure 2. Based on this principle, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains single shared fake model exclusively on the students final generated outputs and uses it to provide correction signals for every denoising step. By aligning the fake models reference with the endpoint distribution, eDMD eliminates the reference residual and ensures that the distribution matching signal is determined by the discrepancy between the teacher and the students final outputs, independently of the intermediate sampling trajectory (Corollary 1). This allows intermediate steps to take whatever form best suits few-step generation, without imposing unnecessary distributional constraints. Beyond correcting the student-side distribution reference, effective DMD also depends on the quality of the supervision provided by the teacher. D-DMD [21] identifies CFG augmentation of the teacher prediction as the primary engine of few-step distillation. However, existing methods typically obtain teacher targets through single guided network evaluation at each sampled noise level. Such predictions can average over multiple plausible outputs and lose fine-grained details, whereas the teacher achieves highquality generation through iterative denoising (Fig. 2, bottom). To improve the precision of teacher supervision, we introduce precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step teacher predictions with short multi-step guided trajectories within the final denoising interval, providing sharper and more accurate supervision without increasing student inference cost. Furthermore, teacher predictions are not equally reliable across noise levels, as guidance and model approximation errors can introduce inconsistencies between predictions at different noise levels. Uniformly sampling noise levels may therefore expose intermediate student steps to unreliable supervision. To address this issue, we introduce calibrated query density that estimates the teachers crosslevel prediction consistency before distillation and concentrates intermediate-step queries on noise levels that provide more reliable supervision. Overall, eDMD aligns the distribution matching objective with the students final outputs and improves the quality of teacher supervision. We evaluate eDMD on four representative diffusion and flow matching backbones (SD3Medium [6], FLUX.2-klein-4B, FLUX.2-klein-9B [2], and Qwen-Image-2.1 [38]), distilling each into 4-step generator without using real images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching baselines, achieving the highest peak HPSv3++ [26] scores across all four backbones. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We identify and theoretically characterize an objective mismatch in multi-step DMD: training the fake model on intermediate predictions introduces reference residual that distorts distribution matching and vanishes if and only if the fake model learns the endpoint distribution. We propose eDMD, which trains shared fake model exclusively on the students final outputs and strengthens teacher supervision through multi-step precise teacher (PT) and calibrated query density. Experiments on four backbones show consistent improvements over existing distribution matching methods, with higher human-preference scores, improved fine-grained details, and fewer structural artifacts. 3 2. Related work 3.1. Multi-step distribution matching Few-step diffusion distillation. Few-step distillation trains student to match the quality of diffusion or flow matching teacher [10, 20, 48] in only few sampling steps. Trajectory-based methods train the student to follow the teachers sampling path: progressive distillation merges adjacent steps [36, 44], rectified flows straighten the path [24, 25], and consistency and flow-map methods learn direct mappings from noisy states to cleaner states [15, 29, 32, 40, 41, 49, 52]. Adversarial methods instead align output distributions using discriminator against real or teacher samples [19, 45, 46]. Distribution matching, which our work builds upon, aligns them using score estimates from the teacher and an online fake model. Distribution matching distillation. Building on score distillation for text-to-3D generation [37, 55], Diff-Instruct and DMD update the student with the score difference between the pretrained teacher and fake model trained online on the students samples [33, 62]. Subsequent work explores alternative divergences [54, 60, 65], incorporates refines the fake score adversarial objectives [31, 61], estimate or the update direction [7, 58], or mitigates mode collapse [18, 56]. DMD2 extends DMD to multi-step generation [61], setting adopted by many later methods [21, 23, 27, 34, 56, 66]. Their fake models are typically trained on intermediate predictions or states, whereas we show that only fake model trained on final outputs avoids biasing the student update. This also explains choice found in some implementations: ADM fits its fake model to final outputs in its training algorithm [31], and the final-step matching variant of SiD supervises only the final output by back-propagating through the entire sampling chain [66], whereas eDMD corrects every step directly. Teacher supervision. Distillation relies on the quality of the teachers supervision. For diffusion models, generation quality often depends on guidance, from CFG [9] and its refinements [17, 42, 53] to guidance by weaker model [14] or by perturbed attention [1]. D-DMD shows that the same holds in DMD: CFG augmentation of the teacher prediction is the primary engine of few-step distillation, with distribution matching acting as regularizer [21]. Strengthening the teachers supervision is therefore direct way to improve the student, for example by fine-tuning the teacher [34], targeting reward-tilted teacher distribution [13], or deriving regression targets from the teachers own denoising outputs [8, 46, 56, 68]. 3. We distill four teachers into 4step students without using real images: SD3-Medium [6], FLUX.2-klein-4B and FLUX.2-klein-9B [2], and QwenImage-2.1 [38]. During distillation, we use each teachers default CFG scale (w = 7 on SD3-Medium, = 4 on the FLUX.2 models, and = 1 on Qwen-Image). On QwenImage, eDMD uses PAG to enhance the teacher predictions (App. F). The SD3-Medium and FLUX.2 runs train on the 191,500 prompts of CDM [23] for 2,000 updates on NPUs; Qwen-Image trains on prompt-enhanced rewrites of these prompts for 600 updates on H800 GPUs (App. C). Baselines. We compare against DMD2 [61], D-DMD [21], TDM [34], and CDM [23], and include the official 4-step FLUX.2-klein models and 8-step Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo as unranked references. DMD2 (without its GAN loss) and D-DMD are trained in our codebase using their released recipes, with learning rates adjusted for SD3-Medium and both FLUX.2 models (App. E). On SD3-Medium, we evaluate the official TDM and CDM checkpoints with their native samplers; on the FLUX.2 models, we retrain CDM and use our ℓ2 re-implementation of TDM, which outperforms Huber loss on FLUX.2-klein-4B. On Qwen-Image, we compare with DMD2 and TDM. Evaluation. We generate 1,000 images from the 200 DrawBench prompts [43] using five seeds per prompt, forming DrawBench-1000. We report HPSv3++ [26], HPSv3 [35], PickScore [16], LAION Aesthetic [47], HPSv2.1 [57], ImageReward [59], CLIP score [39], and DPG-Bench [12]. For each run, we select the peak checkpoint by the highest HPSv3++ over raw and EMA weights evaluated every 100 updates. For SD3-Medium and the FLUX.2 models, we also report raw HPSv3++ at 1k and 2k updates (multiseed and held-out checks in App. G). 5.2. Main results Quantitative comparison.
